utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the courtroom. I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies today. Mr. Tolimir is now commencing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May peace reign in this house, and may these proceedings and today's hearing be concluded in keeping with God's will and not my own. I wish a pleasant stay to Mr. Mitrovic here with us and a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, yesterday you were asked about many topics yesterday. We'll start from the beginning, and you're free to answer the questions I will put to you the way you deem fit. On a number of occasions yesterday, there was discussion of how you were captured. On page 6, as well as page 8, the Prosecutor asked you how you were captured. He even said that tear gas was thrown into your solitary cell. You said that, for you, they were paramilitary -- they were not paramilitary formations. Or I believe the Prosecutor's position was that the Croatian forces at the time were not paramilitary. Why did we consider them to be paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the question. Your Honours, yesterday I said that, for me, they were paramilitary formations and not regular Croatian forces because, at that time, the JNA was still the legal armed force of the state we lived in. That is why I believed them to be paramilitary formations. Otherwise, as I was serving in that garrison in Croatia, I had occasion through my work to receive operational information on the creation of those formations far ahead of the war, much earlier than September 1991. There was also information of -- on how they were arming themselves. That is why I qualified them as paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Can you tell us whether they were paramilitary formations even under the then Croatian constitution as well as under the then SFRY constitution, and since they were paramilitary were their activities illegal under the Croatian law and the SFRY law?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were definitely paramilitary forces, as regards the law of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Whether they were illegal under the then-Croatian constitution, that is something I can't say. Why is that? Those were primarily police forces, forces of the MUP. They established the ZNG as the reserve and active-duty force of the MUP. It was so until, at the stadium in Maksimir when they had their first parade, Tudjman promoted them into some kind of armed forces of the future Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is regular service determined based on one's position within the state structure or because of one's conduct? As you said, the MUP in Croatia was a legal body; however, their activities were illegal because they were not supposed to attack the army under the Croatian and SFRY constitution?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you put it in that context, then it was so. No one mandated them to do this. And the then-JNA was not an enemy force in Croatia at the time when the conflict broke out. The JNA did not do anything to provoke those forces. It did not undertake any anti-constitutional steps which would provide an excuse or reason for those forces to come into action. Of course, I'm referring to the area of Sibenik, because I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the units of the JNA in the area of Sibenik try to separate the so-called paramilitary formations from the Serb population they attacked in the RSK which was later on proclaimed a UN protected area?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely so. Our role was to place ourselves between the paramilitary forces and the Serbs living in the environs and in the town itself, of course. However, it was most pronounced in the nearby villages populated by Serbs. If you recall, Your Honours, it was the time when barricades were being set up and people were fencing themselves off by ethnicity. Entry into Serb or Croatian villages was prevented. And there was much tension. The war was at the door, basically. It was all around, and the antagonism was severe. There was an eruption of nationalism on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, did both the Supreme Commander and the Federal Secretariat ask of us to disarm both the Serbs and Croats in the territory, to collect their weapons and place it in JNA barracks. Do you recall that period and those specific activities?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were asked to do that because -- well, I remember one thing. In the Sibenik garrison, we had received a task, since, in the Presidency of the then-Yugoslavia - perhaps it was already the rump Presidency by that time - in any case, we received a task to have the Romanian produced Kalashnikovs, the so-called Rogonja [phoen] to be taken away from the paramilitary forces and those weapons to be sent to Belgrade so that the people sitting in the Presidency could see for themselves that indeed those weapons were in circulation, and we did so. What happened afterwards? The then member of the Yugoslav Presidency, Stipe Mesic, asked for 48 hours to review the situation and to see for himself whether those Croatian forces were indeed armed. In a way he didn't trust us. Perhaps they all agreed at the top. He got the period. And within those 48 hours, they managed to print out IDs for the reserve police force, and they distributed them to all those who had previously been given weapons illegally. Thus, basically legalizing those weapons. They made all those people who had received weapons members of the MUP, and so our hands were tied. And not only ours, probably of that the state leadership too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Chamber to understand, you said the Kalashnikovs called Rogonja, were these weapons illegally imported from other countries where they were produced into Croatian territory in order to arm the paramilitary formations and the forces of the MUP and Croatian Army? Were we trying to prove that those weapons were not produced in Yugoslavia factories but was imported illegally and was, as such, prone to be seized?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, they were of Romanian production. Such weapons had not existed in the JNA or in the TO or in the police. It means that those weapons were illegally brought in to that part of the state. That is to say, Croatia. There were even some documentaries made about that, about how the weapons were imported. Of course, such weapons had to be seized, as would be the case in any other normal state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a moment ago Stipe Mesic as the Supreme Commander. He, as the Supreme Commander, did he create the preconditions as you just described for the Croatian paramilitary forces to legalise all their activities so as not to violate the then laws and regulations which were in place for all armed formations?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. In my previous answers, I said that they managed to legalise their operation by having legalised the weapons, when the IDs were issued. In that way, they simply prevented us from doing anything. And in my view, it was a wise move. They made any further action against them impossible, and, at the same time, they carried out sieges of all military facilities in the territory of Croatia. And, of course, again, I'm speaking of Sibenik. Not only that. They made our life in the military facilities in Sibenik unbearable. It probably went for all other military facilities as well. They turned off our electricity, water, telephone lines. They brought their children, women there, provoking members of the JNA, primarily those on active duty. They also called for soldiers to desert, and many soldiers did, primarily those who were not Serbs. Next, they put on -- the JNA hall in Sibenik under a siege. They pelted it with stones, and I was actually in the JNA hall with a military police squad when it took place. They demolished the place. When foreign delegations arrived in Sibenik, they screened off the entire JNA hall with blankets and sheets so that they wouldn't see that the building was demolished. They also placed loud-speakers. They played music in front of the barracks which worked round the clock, and invited people to surrender. This was -- amounted to psychological torture and it was a clear message that the Serb members of the JNA were not wanted. That's the summary of the whole story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, may I interrupt you for a moment. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need a clarification to better understand the flow of your evidence. At the beginning -- at the beginning of your evidence, you have made reference to paramilitary and regular forces. In order for me to understand clearly, can you just briefly, very briefly, tell the difference between the paramilitary and regular forces? And then -- maybe I will ask the other question when you have given me your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that the then National Guard Corps in Croatia was, for me, a military formation. Because, at the time, the JNA was the legitimate armed force in Yugoslavia, including the territory of the Republic of Croatia and all other parts of the then Yugoslavia. They were the only legal armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So, therefore, your reference to paramilitary means they were illegal forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question is, at page 3 of today's transcript, line 24, you are recorded as having said: "... people were fencing themselves off by ethnicity." Can you explain that term to me, "fencing themselves off by ethnicity"? What does that mean exactly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I wasn't clear enough. I said that, at the time, barricades were put up in villages. Serbian villages put up barricades, Croatian villages put up barricades. That was the meaning of "fencing off." I also said that there was rampant antagonism. There was an eruption of nationalistic feelings on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So, in other words, people tended to group themselves accord to their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, right. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mitrovic, can you briefly tell us whether paramilitary formations in all areas, including Croatia, Serbia and everywhere, were illegal because of their activities which were illegal and unconstitutional and unlawful in the entire territory of the SFRY? From your professional point of view.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. In your question, you practically included the answer, illegal activities are considered to be paramilitary activities everywhere, whatever is not part of the system. In Republika Srpska, during the war, as the Army of Republika Srpska, we considered the forces which were not under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska to be paramilitary forces, illegal forces, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D797 in e-court so that we could see something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And until then, let me phrase my question: Did the JNA and the members of the army disarm paramilitary formations regardless of the ethnicity, if they were found in a part of the territory that was under its control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, and that was still just the beginning, I'm talking about the period preceding open combat, so before any fighting broke out. If we are talking about that period, our attitude and our criteria were absolutely the same towards the Croats, the Croatian forces, and towards the Serbs. Later on -- perhaps you would ask me that as well. Later on it happened that we had to defend Serbs from the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will ask you immediately, please always answer briefly so that we could manage to do everything. I have not much time and probably you want to go home today. This is my question: Did the federal secretary of national defence make a decision, and the Presidency as well, that all paramilitary formations be disarmed, that Martin Spegelj and other Croatian leaders who had been in charge of arming the paramilitary forces of the MUP and TO to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you want me to expand that I can, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it done and if not, why not, and tell us what you think about that now? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were prevented. I'm saying that from the point of view of the army and the security organs. We were prevented precisely by the legalisation which I talked about earlier, if we have Croatian forces in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And as for the Presidency of SFRY, was there any resistance to the arrest of Spegelj, Boljkovac, and other Croatian leaders who were illegally arming military conscripts in Croatia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, if we had unified Presidency at the time, and a different way of controlling the state, probably the war wouldn't have happened in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us when some of the weapons which arrived from abroad in the so-called Kikas aircraft was seized. Do you remember that and can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that the aircraft was seized, that it was full of weapons, that weapons were unloaded in Belgrade, I think, and that that was the most flagrant material proof or the most obvious one at the time that illegal arming was taking place, that arms were being imported and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, when the conflicts broke out, did the one and the other and the third side begin to arm themselves illegally and set up their paramilitary formations which you also mentioned yesterday? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. When combat activities began to be carried out and there were dead on either side, the arming was stepped up and so was the setting up of paramilitary organisations organising people into such units on either side, which is in a way a normal reaction of any man to defend himself, protect himself so that this was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was anyone prosecuted by the Croatian authorities because of illegal arming and setting up paramilitary formations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it the occasion then for an escalation of violence and illegal conduct in the whole territory of Croatia regardless of the specific areas in question were populated by Serbs or Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Your Honours, perhaps that was one of the causes, but it was obvious that this activity was organised. It was not chaotic, and these were not isolated incidents of a murder of an individual somewhere which caused an entire army to be armed and attacks to be carried out on all facilities. It was an organised activity and the organisation did not begin in 1990 or 1991 but probably sometime earlier. With the multi-party elections in Croatia, there was already talk about Croatia becoming an independent country, a separate country, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. We're interested in the beginning of the war in the territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is why I'm asking you, if one whole republic put up resistance to all the decisions made by the Presidency and the federal secretary of National Defence, did that then reflect on individual unlawful conduct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was reflected in that as well, of course. But if you want us to talk about Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was already in that time, in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, it was, if I may put it so, an example that something similar should be applied, a similar scenario should be applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If that is what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't have that mind. But yesterday during examination-in-chief and in your interview also you were asked by the investigator why were Serbs in Croatia defended. I will ask you to tell us the following: Did the JNA have the task to protect the Serbs in Croatia according to the Vance-Owen Plan or was it doing that just because Kadijevic wanted that and wrote that in an order which was presented to you and which we will have another look at later? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the conflicts in Croatia, the Croats had their forces. They had been already set up. For me they were paramilitary forces, for them they were legal forces; that was the national guard corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Mitrovic. Can something be legal if it's unconstitutional and unlawful?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it cannot be legal if it's unlawful. We already talked about that. But I wanted to finish my thought. The Croats had their own forces. For them they were legal forces, if you like. But not for us. But they could not be legal for them, because they had not been legitimised by the law and by the constitution. This is what I mean. So that's what they had, and the Serbs over there did not have their own army. They had not set it up. And the JNA's task was then to protect them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Mitrovic, you are using the same language and you are talking quite fast. It is very difficult for the interpreters to catch everything, and you can see it especially at the beginning of page 12, that not everything was record the properly because of your overlapping. Please pause between question and answer and the next question. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yeah, just to add on to what Judge Fluegge has said just now, I'm not clear really what your answer is in lines 3 and 4. And it is: "No, it cannot be illegal if it is up lawful." I think we need a clarification there before we move forward because that is quite important. Your answer is quite important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that something that is unlawful is also illegal. I'm not sure how that was translated. I did not say that what is unlawful is not illegal. Because as you say, it's a negation of a negation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is exactly what we heard in the translation. Thank you very much for this clarification. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on. And please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry that we did not correct this. I apologise to the e-court because I called for a wrong document. I wanted 1D794, because we still have not moved to this subject, the war in Bosnia. We're still discussing the war in Croatia. So could we please show 1D794. And I apologise for the slip of the tongue and the error which I made. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, we can see here that the 9th Corps command received from the federal secretary at the time a document or, rather, a directive, and it says here: "Enclosed: Please find the directive of the federal secretary for national defence on the use of armed forces in the coming period." Please tell us briefly for the record, what is a "directive" in the military sense of the word? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, a directive is, to put it in a simplified manner, an order but an order from the higher command organs. That is to say, the Main Staff, the Supreme Command. At our level, it was the Main Staff, or at the time when we are talking about this document, it was the federal secretary or the Federal Secretariat of the National Defence, which is to say that is the level of the Ministry of Defence. A directive is a document, an order, issued at that strategic level. What is just a simple order at the level of a corps or brigade or lower levels, this is how it is called at the strategic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the next page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see now here in the title: "Directive on the Use of Armed Forces in the Coming Period for the Preparation and Carrying out of Combat Operations." My question is this: Were we all obliged by law to apply this directive in the period of preparing for conducting combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were. At all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please turn to the next page? That's page 2 of the document. The first paragraph. I will quote. General Kadijevic says this in the directive: "Our armed forces are entering a new extremely important period of achieving the final goals of the war. Protection of the Serbian population, a peaceful resolution of the Yugoslav crisis, and creating conditions for preserving Yugoslavia for those peoples who want to live in it. That is why preserving the combat readiness of the Yugoslav People's Army and the armed forces in their entirety is still the focal task of all levels of control and command and its members, until such a time when a political resolution to the Yugoslavia crisis is achieved." And further on, he issues the tasks in accordance with this preamble. My question is this: Can we conclude on the basis of the quotation I just read out what the task and the duty of the JNA in Croatia was until the moment when the Vance-Owen Plan was accepted, and could you see that from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I listened very carefully to this line of questions. Some, especially the role of the paramilitaries, was dealt with during the examination-in-chief, but I would like to know what is the relevance for our case in -- in relation to this document and the political tasks and targets at that time in 1991. It's far, far earlier than the relevant time to the indictment. Could you please explain that? This was, if I'm not mistaken, [sic] part of the examination-in-chief yesterday. And I'm referring to these political questions and not referring to the paramilitaries Mr. Thayer dealt with yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yesterday there was some discussion about this topic, and Mr. Mitrovic was even in his answers saying that there weren't only Croats in the army but also Muslims, including Dudakovic, who was chief of artillery. He was earlier asked by an investigator why they were only protecting the Serbs and that was because the Serbs were under attack from the Croatian state, and I'm providing the basics that stem from the statement made by General Kadijevic. I believe this is of great importance. These are the beginnings of the war in Yugoslavia. If somebody stops listening to the state, what can we expect from various individuals? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are right, that some of these topics were raised during examination-in-chief. However, using your court time properly in favour of your Defence should take into account what we are dealing with. We are dealing with the indictment against you, the charges of severe crimes and not the outbreak of the war. Please bear that in mind and use your time carefully. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will, as always, make sure to complete my examination in time and I will give up on some other questions but this one not. This is an important topic. If an individual is behaving unlawfully, that's a small thing, but when a state is behaving like that, that causes a lot of difficulties. I will not deal with that issue too much. Of course, I will just put another question to Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the Vance plan reached in Croatia for the purpose of protection of the Serbian population and were the United Nations the only force that was protecting the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. The plan was reached for the protection of the Serbian population and the United Nations forces were deployed within Croatia for that very purpose, to protect the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And, at the end of the war, when Croatia attacked the protected areas in Croatia, did, at the time, UNPROFOR abandon the positions and stop protecting the protected areas, and did even the NATO forces use air-strikes against these territories?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Tolimir. On line 16 and 17 of page 15, one very important word was left out when I asked you about the relevance of your questioning. I said: "This was, if I'm not mistaken, not part of the examination-in-chief yesterday." The word "not" was left out. I wanted to put that on the record. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mitrovic, could you please tell us whether the Serbian people in Croatia, as well as in other parts of former SFRY, see the Vance Plan as a way of disarming the Serbs who would then, after that, become victims of the same people who disarmed them?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, yes, that's what the people believed. I agree with your words. People felt like that, they felt betrayed not only by the United Nations, but primarily by Serbia, a state that signed the agreement and was there as a guarantee. They were disappointed by what later happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now move to 1995 and the end of the war. At that time, the plan, the so-called Z-4 plan, was being in the process of making, the mediator was Peter Galbraith, an American Ambassador in Croatia, which was finally agreed upon before the Operation Storm in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that plan and I do remember what it was supposed to create.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise for the transcript. Could you tell me whether you remember that immediately one day after the Z-4 plan was agreed upon, whether the Croatian Army started their Operation Storm against the protected areas in Croatia. In other words, areas where the Serbs lived?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember that the same Peter Galbraith, American ambassador, was seen on Croatian tanks? Did you see such photos later on after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. The war in Croatia and the Operation Storm is not part of this trial. Please bear that in mind and don't waste time. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do answer, Mr. Mitrovic. This was directly linked up with the area of responsibility of your corps.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see the photograph, but I do know I've heard in the period after the war about the role of Peter Galbraith in that operation and the preparations of this Operation Storm, that was something one could find in the media. All my knowledge stems from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just briefly in one sentence tell us all that you know and then we will move to other topics.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In simple terms, in our military terminology, the Croats got the green light from the Americans and all the necessary assistance for the purpose of resolving the Serbian question in the parts of Croatia called Serbian Republic of Krajina within seven days. They were promised they will receive American support and that there will be no strong reactions condemning such an operation. That's all I can say briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir, you should have realised that the witness said "... all my knowledge stems from there," which means from the media. How can that help your Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness could not have been in Croatia at that time because he would have been killed, and the media demonstrated what the objective was of the negotiations, the Z-4 negotiations. We could have only seen Galbraith riding a tank if Croatian television broadcast such images. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you should indeed move to relevant topics, relevant to this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Let's start with the relevant topic. In 1995, the Croatian Army attacked the zone of your corps. Could you tell us in just a few sentences how numerous were the Croatian forces and from which directions did they launch their attack against Bosnia and Herzegovina, attacking the zone of the 2nd Krajina Corps where you were serving?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late 1995, in other words, June, July, and August of 1995, the legal units of Croatian Army took part in the so-called Operation Maestral. In other words, they were carrying out activities along two axes. One was Livno-Grahovo axis which was in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps and the other axis was Livno-Glamoc axis. And they also carried out activities along the axis Sipovo-Mrkonjic Grad entering into both of these towns; in other words, Sipovo and Mrkonjic Grad. These were mainly forces of the Croatian Operative Zone Split. I cannot tell you which brigades these were. I know about the Sinj Regiment, but can I cannot remember, as I sit here, their numerical denomination. But I do remember that we managed to capture a major from that unit who was a logistics assistant in this Sinj Regiment, and later on he was exchanged. But all in all, they were active along the axis I mentioned a moment ago and now I'm speaking about the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps. I must add that prior to that the Croatian forces were also active in Kupres area in 1992. I'm talking about the Croatian Army. Up until the 7th of April, I believe, of 1992, they were there, present in the Kupres area, carrying out active operations against Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you are talking about Croatian forces and Serbian forces, did you mean Croatian forces from Bosnia and Herzegovina or from the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was talking about Kupres, both of these were present. When I was talking about the other axis, or, to be more precise, when I was talking about the axis of activity in 1995, again, there were both units of the Croatian Army and the units of the HVO active there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise, I understood you initially as well, but for the sake of transcript, we must make sure that it's clearly stated where did the Croatian forces come from. Could you please tell us were there any NATO air-strikes against Serbian forces that occurred during the Maestral -- the operation Maestral that was being carried out by the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. There were some activities carried out by the NATO air force against some of the positions and some more important elements of the combat disposition of the VRS also in the zone of the 2nd Krajina Corps. These were mainly strikes against radio relay hubs and nodes and some of the elevations where these were located. That was something that was happening almost simultaneously. I don't know whether it was a synchronised operation, but it ask likely that it was done in agreement between Croatia and NATO but I cannot make a conclusion to that effect, but the NATO activities did assist, or, rather, speed up the breakdown of the zones of responsibility of the 1st and the 2nd Krajina Corps. At the time, we were receiving information through intelligence channels to the effect that some NATO rapid reaction forces were carrying out artillery attacks against our command posts and such more important areas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Because you cannot make such a conclusion; namely, a conclusion that it was in a co-ordinated -- oh, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it might be helpful to see how the last answer links up with other testimony which the Trial Chamber has already heard. If we could just get some orientation to date for these activities, because right now it's in a temporal vacuum. I think it might be helpful if Colonel Mitrovic could provide an approximate date, month, for these activities that he just described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Also, for the Chamber, it would be helpful to understand this topic better. Please clarify that with the witness, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mitrovic, you just told us that you cannot conclude whether the activities were co-ordinated or not. Could you please tell Mr. Thayer when exactly did that happen, because yesterday he also asked you about the transfer of information through Neven system, and I would like to ask you now to tell us whether this Neven system existed throughout any specific period, and also please tell us at which time period did NATO attack VRS positions in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did explain that but I will repeat. It was June, July, August, and September, during that period in 1995 - and we are talking about 1995 - we're talking about the end of the war, because in your question you specified we were talking about 1995 and Operation Storm, so I assumed that we all understood we're talking about 1995. But it was during those months that we had the zone of -- no flying zone and even then there were certain NATO attacks against radio relay facilities and communication systems. Thank you nor reminding me. Yesterday we were talking about Neven and now can I explain why we could not set up the Neven system within our zone, and one of the reasons was precisely that; namely, Klekovaca radio relay facility had been destroyed prior to that, which was our main radio relay system.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now the interpretation has stopped. Once again, sir, Mr. Mitrovic, I quote from your penultimate answer. You said, I quote: "At the time we were receiving information through intelligence channels to the effect that some NATO rapid reaction forces were carrying out artillery attacks against our command posts." When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was discussing the period of June, July, August, and September of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mitrovic, let's look at D259, which refers to the very reasons why the Neven system was inoperational and why the teleprinter connections were down. This is a document about the changes in the communications system, as well as establishing a courier system. It states here that the 2nd Krajina Corps received it as well. It states: "Due to the partially inoperational communications system which was caused by NATO aeroplane air-strikes against radio relay hubs and PTT facilities in the areas of responsibility of the SRK, HK, DK, and IBK and until other alternative communication routes are established, in order to have the teletype traffic established, I order ..." And here we see the various items of the order which states that from your area, that of the 1st Bosnian Corps, mail was to be delivered by couriers, and from there, it would be -- from the other corps it would be picked up to be taken to the Main Staff. Do you recall this period? The document was signed by General Ratko Mladic. If we go to the next page, we'll see the signature block. You can see it there. Since the order was issued in September 1995, can you tell us whether, at the time, there could have been any communication between any corps commands and Tolimir through the Neven system, as you were asked yesterday at page 38 and 39?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, before providing an answer, I'd like to clarify one thing. Namely, the 2nd Krajina Corps, on its northern borders, neighboured on the Republic of the Serb Krajina, as long as it existed. Following Operation Storm, which began on August 1, 1995, the RSK and its army no longer existed. The 2nd Krajina Corps received another 180 kilometres of front lines, so we were basically adjacent to the Croat and Muslim forces. When I say Croat forces, I have in mind both the HVO and the Croatian Army. In other words, the situation was completely new. On the other hand, there were NATO air-strikes, and by that time it became increasingly difficult to fight and offer any resistance. There were also operations against radio relay hubs, radar stations, and other facilities. This all caused a breakdown in the system of command and control. A consequence of that was this very order, which tried to establish a different communications system. This September of 1995 order basically confirms what I said yesterday concerning the Neven system in my corps. I also said that, most likely, the other corps which had not moved retained the system. However, I now see that they, too, had problems. This is the only answer I can provide you with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at 1D776 next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering D259?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As there is no translation, it will be marked for identification, pending translation. One moment, please, we need a document -- no, sorry, I made a mistake. I was referring to D258 -- 9, but this is already an exhibit. It was my mistake. Sorry for that. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mitrovic, before us is a document of the 30th of August, 1995. The title is: "NATO Aircraft Activities in the Areas of Responsibility of the Corps Specified." And then it says: "Information." It was forwarded to your command, among others. It states: "Early in the morning on the 30th of August 1995, NATO forces carried out two comprehensive air-strikes against targets chosen beforehand. The first strike took place between 1.40 and 2.40 hours with 40 planes of which 30 were assault planes. Combat itself lasted for some ten minutes. The second comprehensive strike included 30 planes." The third paragraph: "During these two comprehensive strikes, the enemy was active in the general area of the Command Staff of the VRS without causing any damage there. They also attacked the radar position at RRC Jahorina, Stolica and Kmur, the PTT relay hub Strazica Cajnice, Trebevic, former RRC Zlovrh, and firing positions of the rocket battery Kuh [phoen] in the general area of Sokolac." My question is this: If NATO was attacking all communications centres, including that of the Main Staff, and of the corps, was it possible to keep communication between the Main Staff and the corps by using the Neven system which we discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course, it was impossible. There were many problems and that is why the order we saw a moment ago was issued seeking for alternative solutions to be established. Of course, an armed forces must not be left without its communication abilities. As a system it has to have alternative solutions in place, otherwise it cannot survive without this communication between superiors and subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. I will show you 65 ter document number 05834. It is an OTP document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Registrar told me that the document, 1D776, we have on the screen, was already MFI'd pending translation as D257. But it's not listed in your list of documents to be used during cross-examination, if I'm not mistaken. That creates, sometimes, quite a bit of confusion. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is possible that I mixed up some documents. We can see the other document on the screen now. It is dated the 11th of October, 1995, which is only a day later, following ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see here that it was sent to your corps. The title is: "Blocking the Enemy Offensive on the Western RS Front. Order:" It is stated here what unit and what officer were to do in order to carry it out. Certain locations are thereby established.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can go onto the next page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at the bullet points to see which officers were placed where, in order to implement this order to stop the offensive. First we have the Chief of Staff; then his assistant, General Gvero; next, is Assistant commander for the air force; and the assistant commander for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel; followed by assistant commander for intelligence and security, Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. Just below that we see where it says Mrkonjic Grad, village of Trijebovo, village of Stricici, and is responsible for the defence of the axis, meaning that I was in the area of responsibility of the 30th Infantry Division in Mrkonjic Grad. Do you recall that period, and did you know that I was in Mrkonjic Grad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just for the record, sometimes, indeed, you are confusing all of us. The document on the screen which is 65 ter 5834 was previously tendered by you and is already in evidence as D264 as listed in your list of documents to be used during cross-examination. Please try to give us the right reference. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise. It seems I have hard copies which need not necessarily reflect those in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case my question is this: Mr. Mitrovic, were all of the organs of the Main Staff engaged in the western theatre in order to block the Croatian offensive Maestral and the NATO offensive which included rapid reaction forces as the land force -- strike forces?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was customary in our army that when in a certain part of the front there is significant incursion by the enemy that someone from the command would get there. In this case, people from the Main Staff came to the corps command and those from the corps command went down to brigade commands and so on down to the level of battalion. In this situation, I recall General Tolimir, in the period between July 1995 and October 1995, coming to the area of the 2nd Krajina Corps. I also recall him being there before and following the fall of Glamoc, since he hails from that area. He was before and following the fall of Drvar sometime in September along the Glamoc-Drvar axis. Since in this particular case our units were adjacent, he was in Manjaca in October along the axis stipulated in the order; that is to say, Mrkonjic Grad, Glamoc, and Stricici. We met on those occasions and that is why I can address this issue. I cannot specify any dates and please don't hold me to any, but it was in that period in the course of those few months, September and October.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Could you please repeat all of the months you mentioned because during your answer you mentioned August as well when Glamoc fell. So in what months was I there?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat, Your Honours. In July, before and after Glamoc fell, because General Tolimir was born in a village near Glamoc. Glamoc fell on the 27th of July. Next, in September, before and after Drvar fell; Drvar fell on the 14th or 15th of September. This also includes the period in October by which we, as the corps, were about to expire, so to say. It is directly connected to this order. It was probably sometime around the middle of the month. The only precise thing I can tell you is what I told you about the 27th of July and the 14th and 15th of July, as well as the date around the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you remember whether I was in your AOR and at your command post when the RSK fell and as their forces were leaving it?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in early August. You were there, as well as General Mladic. There were a number of generals from the Main Staff there. There were also meetings with General Mrksic who, at the time, was the commander of the RSK army. You also met with his staff in order to arrange accommodation and reception of the soldiers and population and to see whether there were any possibilities to consolidate the ranks of the ARSK. We also had to collect the equipment which had been left behind by the Army of the RSK along various routes because they were withdrawing in complete chaos. All these events are mutually linked and it is difficult to recall specifically each and every one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mitrovic, later, on page 41, you were asked about, unless I'm mistaken it was the subject of command and control. The Prosecutor asked you whether Tolimir was your superior, and you said that the corps commander was your commander and "Tolimir controlled me in the professional sense." Can you please explain to us now whether the command system was unified and single in the whole Army of Republika Srpska and was the principle of unity of command something that was applied? And then can you tell us what was the place of specialised organs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was subordination in the entire Army of Republika Srpska. I would say that only after the consolidation of the army this was established. There were problems at the beginning, in 1992, until all the command and control systems were set up, in accordance with rules and regulations and until they began to function. Not everything was nice as defined by the rules which were then in force. There were problems. There was anarchy in some places. All sorts of things. But, later, I would say in late 1992 or early 1993, it was already a stable system, in which it was known who was in charge of what.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. As you want to talk about the period when not everything was all right, can we please show you the document 1D797 so that we could discuss this. It's an information from the Main Staff dated the 28th of July, 1992, report on paramilitary formations in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This report has several pages. I signed it and sent it to the corps commands. I saw from your interview with the Prosecutor which was submitted by the Prosecution. And can you tell me whether you remember the contents of this report, whether you read it, and whether you received it in the first place? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do remember the contents of this report. The report includes a detail about a person from the 2nd Krajina Corps. That is included in the report. And the report, as you can see, dates from July 1992. That means two months after the beginning of setting up or, in fact, two and a half months, or three, after the beginning of the setting up of the Army of Republika Srpska. And paramilitary forces, paramilitary units, were a problem which had to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show page 4 to the witness so that he could see paragraph 5, if that's what he had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says: "In the area of the Kljuc municipality: Revival of paramilitary formations can be seen. The units formed in this area are commanded by the self-styled vojvoda, Jovo Kevac, who incited a rebellion in the Stricici educational centre in late April --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... slowing down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And so on. "Prevented the sending of 117 conscripts and reserve officers ... to the war units, at the Kljuc battalion ..." Was this what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is precisely what I had in mind. I'm sorry that we did not perhaps leave out the name because of this person, because later on he somehow came to, if I can put it that way, and he was a member of the unit completely normal and regular. There is another matter I wish to note in terms of the paramilitary forces. These paramilitary forces sometimes came when invited by certain persons from certain municipalities. It was without the knowledge and without the approval of the unit commands. I know what happened in the corps zone of responsibility. And what happened when those paramilitary forces whose morale was low and who were recruited from specific social groups and who were prone to many immoral acts. When they started making problems with the local population, then there would be problems, because then there would be requests made to the military that such paramilitary forces be disarmed or chased away from the territory and so on. And this is actually what we did. We treated them as requested in this record and how it was regulated by the rules, even earlier. I'm talking about the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. I apologise for mentioning the name of this person, but this was an occasion for you to say what deserves to be said about him. I know that later on in accordance with this report he was integrated into the army and became one of the better soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please turn the page and show the last page of this report. It is page 6 in the document, rather than page 35. That is it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would read just the last paragraph: "The presence and activity of paramilitary formations has a two-fold negative influence on the Serbian people. The people are losing their trust in the authorities and they're losing the power to deal with the war profiteers, criminals, and mass murders. And, secondly, it, to a large degree, demoralises the members of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, discouraging the fighting and often resulting in the abandonment of positions. Every armed Serb in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina must be placed under the exclusive command of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina Army or else he should be disarmed and legal measures taken." I signed this and it was sent to all security departments, also to the president of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the prime minister, and the army Main Staff commander so that they would measures against individual you mentioned and against others as well. Can you please tell us this: When all those who carried out paramilitary activities are integrated within the system and when measures are applied to them, then would every unit be responsible for them if they are integrated in them and the authorities would be responsible for those persons who were not part of the system of the JNA or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, in accordance with this order. And otherwise the attitude was that whoever wanted to fight, really, and who had come as a volunteer - because usually they would all come labelled as volunteers - whoever wanted to fight, they could fight together with the units. Those who didn't want had to leave the units, they had to hand in their weapons and their military equipment and they would be either transported outside of the zone of this corps or, alternatively, handed over to the civilian authorities so that they would treat this person as they deemed fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm sorry, we must have our first break now. And we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, and Mr. Mitrovic, on behalf of the interpreters, I would kindly ask you to slow down. You are very well trained army officers and fast speakers, and it's very difficult for the interpreters. You must realise they have to catch everything in your language, then translate into English. From there, it is sometimes interpreted into French. And everything has to be recorded in our transcript. This is a very difficult task, and both parties and the Chamber has to rely on the transcript, that everything is correctly recorded. So please bear that in mind. Slow down while speaking, especially while reading from a document, and pause between question and answer and the next question. Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We apologise once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, we have looked at 1D797. We have seen that it was submitted to both the civilian and military authorities in the republic in order to resolve the problems we wrote about in 1992. Can you tell us whether you also acted in accordance with this document in your zone, once you received it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course we acted in accordance with this order. We had to implement it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. This was a report signed by me which was submitted to the following addresses which we can see here. Can we please have that admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then we will move on to the order in accordance with which you acted while disarming paramilitaries in your zone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document on the screen, 1D797, will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D797, shall be assigned Exhibit D274. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And that is the number I used. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we now please show 1D796. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Until the document appears on the screen, I should say it is a document issued by the Main Staff of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 29th of July, 1992. It is an order which says: "Disarmament of Paramilitary Formations. Order:" It is an order of General Mladic in accordance with which you acted. Can you see it now, and you can see that General Mladic informs the commanders, and, for example, he says in the first paragraph: "The analysis of paramilitary organisation in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina established that paramilitary formations exist in areas of responsibility of all the corps and are mainly located behind the lines of combat activities, in the rear, and in inhabited areas." And so on and so forth. Can we now please show the second page in which he explains what needs to be done. We can see that it was sent to the commands of all corps as well as to the President of the Presidency and the prime minister for their information. This is what he orders, but it is on the third page. So can we please show that one now. Page 3. We'll only look at item 1 in which the general says: "All paramilitary formations and their leaders, if their intentions truly are honourable, are to place themselves in the service of the just struggle for the survival of the Serbian people, and are to offer to incorporate themselves into regular ... army units of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to be deployed in accordance with their military specialities and level of military training." We'll now also read item 3: "Paramilitary formations, groups, and individuals from their composition who refuse to be placed under unified SRBiH Army command are to be disarmed and arrested in co-operation with the MUP, and criminal proceedings are to be initiated against them for crimes they committed." Item 7 says: "I will hold the corps commanders in their areas of responsibility and the SRBiH Army Main Staff chief of intelligence and security affairs responsible for the implementation of this order. Commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic." This is my question: Did the commander of the Main Staff clearly inform by this order both the military and political structures that he wanted to place everyone under the control of the army or imprison those who acted in a contrary manner?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I confirm that Mr. Tolimir is right. The order clearly informed us about what we are supposed to be doing, not only us, but also other organs within the territory. Even before this order, the paramilitary formations were a problem for us. They prevented us from carrying out everyday combat activities. We didn't need to have them and deal with them in the rear and have some of our forces involved in activities on disarmament of such units and removal of these people from our area of responsibility. The priority for us was the front line and not their activities in the rear. In brief, we acted in accordance with this order. At least in the zone of our corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. In case of a problem within the units or within the territory, did all law enforcement organs there have to report via official channels about such unlawful actions by the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the VRS members, yes; if you are referring to MUP and other security structures on the territory of Republika Srpska, I assume it was the same. They most probably were also duty-bound to report to their ministries and their superiors about such events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked yesterday about some events that took place in the territory, such as arson of mosques and so on, and you were also asked what your actions were in order to respond. And my question to you now is: Was anyone duty-bound to report about such events, or was it sufficient for someone to simply notice it while touring the area?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were reports about combat activities. I never came across in any of the written reports submitted by our units, reports about a mosque being destroyed, mosque or some other religious facility that belonged to any of the confessions there. What we would see was reports about destruction of Orthodox religious facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On several occasions yesterday, for instance, on page 24, you said that only in the professional sense you were under the security organs' control from the superior command and that you were, throughout the period, under the command of your own commander. So to avoid any ambiguities, let me ask you whether you were subordinated to your commander in relation to tasks that you had been given by your superior along the professional line of security? Were you responsible to the commander for such activities as well?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because my superior would inform my commander that I had failed to carry out a task received from him. The commander was the one who could use various measures after someone failed to carry out his tasks. The superior security organ did not have that at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether the commander of any unit, including the corps level or the Main Staff level, has all legal measures and forces at his disposal for the purpose of carrying out everything that he is entitled to, according to his command position; and are there any exceptions, in relation to this, when we're talking about any level within the corps or the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules of service of the security organ, the security organ was under the commander of the unit in which he is serving. That automatically means that the commander had at his disposal all various elements for resolving any problems. It was a different thing how the resolution of a problem would be accomplished. I would like to add that security organs within units were not untouchables.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document that was on the screen just a moment ago. The order issued by General Mladic, 1D796. And then we would like to move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just wait, wait, wait, wait, wait, wait, please. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D796 shall be assigned exhibit number D275. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before we move on from this document, I'm hoping to save just a little bit of time, and maybe we can have an agreement from the Defence on this. With respect to this document - and I noticed it with this document and a previous document - the heading states that the name of the army is the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm not sure if the Trial Chamber has heard much testimony to this effect, but I think both parties can agree that that was the name of the army prior to its naming itself or renaming itself, the Army of Republika Srpska, or VRS. Same army, different name, just earlier in the war. I'm not sure again if we're heard testimony about that, but I think that's something we can probably agree on or perhaps we could put the question to Colonel Mitrovic. Rather than bringing it up again on re-direct, I thought we could just save some quick time and clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. We saw at least two documents with this term, "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Mr. Mitrovic, can you help us with this? Is this the same unit, the same army, as it was called later, the Army of the Republika Srpska, VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is the same army, the same units initially; in other words, in mid-1992, at the time when the Army of Republika Srpska was established, that was on the 12th of May. I realise I speeded up again. I'll slow down. So on the 12th of May, 1992, the Republika Srpska was called Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to tender the document that's on our screens. Thank you. Thank you. Can we now please have 1D783. This is the statement of our witness given to the investigators on the 17th of June, 2004. We can see it on our screens now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is sometimes difficult for me to get the floor because the translation or something else has -- was continuing. I just wanted to clarify you said on line 21 of page 41: "I would like to tender the document." It was tendered and it was admitted into evidence as D275. It was not marked. It was admitted as D275. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The document that we can see here is identical to OTP document 65 ter 2785, and I would like to ask the secretary to present this document that's on the said location, namely, 2785. It's an identical document. And for the sake of clarity, we're tendering it. It will make things easier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, it is not quite clear yet. 65 ter 2785, is that the same as 1D783?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the same document the Prosecution has used yesterday without tendering it yet. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move to page 90 of this document, please. Page 86 in the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the second line in the Serbian version you're saying the following: "Security and intelligence organ are under immediate command of the commander of the unit or institution within which they are located, but in the professional sense they are controlled by the security and intelligence organs of the superior command. This indicates their full independence in the implementation of intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks and operative combinations." Bearing in mind that they are subordinated to the commander also for implementing or failing to implement tasks received by their professional superior, could you please clarify this. Would you agree that they're responsible to the commander for all assignments, even those that were received from the professional superiors from the superior command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the text read out by General Tolimir is a quotation from the rules of service of the security organs which I referred to on several occasions today as well, where it is clearly defined who's responsible to whom and how the command and control over the security organs is carried out. I am not quite clear as to what's unclear. If I could be assisted by getting a more precise, better-defined question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your answer, lines 2 to 9, in line 5 it is stated that the organs of superior command -- yes: "This indicates their full independence in the implementation of intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks and operative combinations." And this is my question: Does that mean that they are completely independent or are they still responsible to the commander and whether they have to justify their successful or unsuccessful implementation of tasks?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the sentence just quoted, one can find reference to the most specifically professional segment of the security organs' work, application of methods by the security organs. Of course, if they failed to succeed in such tasks, the commander must know and does know about it, because they are informed about it by superior security officer. The corps commander is the lowest level at which secret methods of the security organs' work is being approved in cases when certain security problems are being resolved. In practical terms, what does that mean? My superior informs the corps commander whether I have successfully carried out a task. He is the person who has the competence who can assess my work. So he can report to the commander whether I have carried out my task in accordance with the methods prescribed by our service. According to the same logic, on the levels below me, I would be the one who would inform the commander of the brigade that his security officer succeeded or failed to succeed in resolving a security problem. Is that what you had in mind, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. This is precisely what I had in mind. I wanted to have it clear on the record. We will quote another part of the text in the interview to the OTP, where you confirm what you've said already. It is lines 23 through 31. Actually 24. You say that it is Article 18 and then you quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please tell us where we can find the relevant part in the English. Always helpful, especially for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 18. But my legal assistant tells me that it was not fully accurately interpreted. That is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was reading from line 24 in the Serbian, which corresponds to line 3 on the page we see on the screen in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is page 87 in English in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to prepare your cross-examination, together with your assistant, in a proper way so that we don't lose time to find the relevant part on the screen. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll -- I'd be happy to. But we are always short of time because our contact is limited. We have limited contact during a witness 's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says here -- and this is Article 18 where it says: "The security organs of the superior command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces are in charge, expertly speaking, of the ... or are running ... or are in charge of the organs, security organs in the subordinate units. Let me clarify that. So, I'm subordinate to General Boric and I'm responsible to him for my activities, for my entire activities. I told you yesterday that in the time of war, the corps commander is the one who approves the methods, like, you know, secret correspondence, things like that. So, I'm just saying that just to confirm what I said yesterday, that it's the corps commander to whom I'm responsible for my activities." My question is this: Is, in all cases, a commander responsible to his superior commander for any activity of his commands's security organ irrespective of its positive or negative outcome?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, before answering, I'd like to say something about the translation of the interview. There seems to be a -- one negation too many. So it should be that the secrecy of letters is no longer in effect. In other words, secret methods violate those principles of secrecy. The question General Tolimir put is linked to one of my previous answers, when I said that the security organs were not beyond reach. Specifically in my corps, there was a case in which we suggested to the Main Staff that the chief of security in the brigade be removed because he was in conflict with the brigade commander. It was of personal -- a personal nature, and its consequence was that a situation was created in which the security organ no longer reported to his brigade commander, even when it came to general security issues. Once that was spotted, the removal occurred because, we realized, that the security organ was plain wrong and that he conducted himself unprofessionally in the exercise of his duties as part of the brigade command. It was our conclusion, therefore, that the brigade commander was right to complain about his work. Now how was he replaced or removed? The brigade commander complained to the corps commander and myself regarding the conduct of his security organ. The corps commander, on my proposal, forwarded a proposal to the Main Staff and to General Tolimir to have the security officer removed. It was, indeed, done. General, sir, I used this example, trying to answer this question of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel. Let's look at page 91, which is the next page in the Serbian version, where, in lines 2 through 5 you say the following. "I'm stating this to confirm what I said yesterday, which is that the corps commander is the level at which I was -- or to whom I was answerable for my work professionally speaking. However, Colonel Beara was in charge of me, and my second superior officer was General Tolimir." In order to have a precise transcript and precise terminology, I wanted to ask you this: Was your second superior Tolimir or was he two steps up from you, professionally speaking? Was he your superior; that is to say, was he from your -- or was he from your superior command?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the accused is right. I didn't ponder this in such detail as you have just specified. I simply followed the logic of line of subordination. That is why I said that, professionally speaking, you were my second superior. That is to say, two steps up. Professionally speaking, my first superior was the chief of the security administration.
