Since he was your subordinate, I was your subordinate too. In other words, you were my superior two levels up and that is what I was trying to say in my answer. It was accepted as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us be perfectly clear for the record: Are the security organs of a superior command those professional organs which direct the activities of security organs one step down, say, in the brigade? Is it better to say that these are the professional organs of the superior command or the organs of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps it may well be more correct, the superior organs in the Main Staff. But in our everyday parlance we used terminology I did. It was easier, in a way. And yet it entailed what you are now addressing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We'll see in the rules that what you say is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're on this statement, let's look at page 87 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 82 in the English version. I'm not sure this is the right page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here you say in line 1: "So, Tolimir could issue orders to the forces?" And then your answer: "Security organs ..." So first I quoted the Prosecutor's question, to which you answered: "Security organs and the intelligence organs." And then we have another question: "Including the military police?" And my question is this: Did the superior command organ issue orders to the organs of the military police in a subordinate command?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have touched upon that issue yesterday. He could issue orders to the military police but once they were approved by the superior commander; however, that only applied to equipment and training. It seems I'm too fast again. In other words, he couldn't order a MP battalion to engage in combat. He couldn't do that. Because the unit commander is the one who is directly subordinated to the commander of the unit in which he is serving. It is defined as per the security service manual, as well as the rules of service for the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would it not be correct to say, then, that the security organ of the superior commander could professionally direct the security organs and the military police in its subordinate command, and it probably did so through the organs of that command.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, are you right. Perhaps my terminology was a bit rough when I said "orders." But this is what we understood your documents to be. Anything coming from you or the Main Staff was considered as such. In any case, this correction of yours is more precise, to properly describe the relationship we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise to you. I simply want to be precise for the transcript and for the sake of the Chamber because, in the first sentence, it seems that the investigator understood that Tolimir could order forces to do something. Could Tolimir order forces at all or could you order anything to the forces of your corps?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, no assistant at any level, assistant commander, this is what I mean, had no authority under any rule, tactical rule, to command forces. Such authority and responsibility lay exclusively with the commander. As assistant commanders, we could propose, or suggest, as professionals. We could propose that a MP unit be used. The chief of artillery, because we were at the same level as the chiefs of branches, could propose use of artillery. The chief of armoured units could propose how the tanks and combat vehicles were to be used. That was the logic followed at that level, by which we could propose anything to the unit commander.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: In line 4, there's a double negation which shouldn't be there. So "had authority under any rule."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this document, 1D783. Perhaps we may use it again later, but I would now move to another document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I note the interpreter's note, the double negation. But I see it in e-court in page 50, line 5 and 6, instead of 4. This is perhaps again a difference between LiveNote and e-court. This document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2785 shall be assigned Exhibit D276. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we now have a look at D203. When we see the first page, we might then skip to page 10 in Serbian and page 11 in English. On this page, this rule, which the witness mentioned, is confirmed. We'll be looking at point 23. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please have a look at this: "An officer of a security organ of a command, unit, institution, or staff of the armed forces provides specialist management for a military police unit. He recommends the use of the military police unit to the senior officer of the command, unit, institution, or staff, and he is responsible to him for the state and activity of the unit." The next paragraph of this point says: "In managing the military police unit, the security organ officer under paragraph 1 of this item has the same rights and duties as officers of arms, services of commands, units, institutions, and staffs of the armed forces in managing units of the arms and services of those commands, units, institutions, or staffs." This is my question. As you explained what we now confirmed by this rule in your previous answer, please just tell us this: Does a security organ have any other rights in relation to the unit of which it is an organ as compared to others in the command?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it has no other rights. Because everyone's right is precisely defined and set out in the rules and instructions of everyone in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you noticed that in the interviews, for example, conducted by investigators with the security organs, these security organs are treated differently than other commands or institutions. For example, artillery organs and so on. Have you noticed that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer about other security organs or interviews between the investigators and other security organs. But I can say that not just the investigators but also our own military structures, as you well know, individuals who were not directly connected with the security organ work and did not control security organs, said something different. They would say that we were above the command, that we were above the commander. Such things. Let me not mention something uglier, like that we are spies and so on. But, anyhow, these are, in my view, individuals who did not understand or know, or probably did not even want to know, what were the security organ's activities in the JNA and later on in the VRS. Because one and the same rules were in force in both.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now that we are on this page. Let us have a look at point 25. Thank you. Can you also please show point 25 in English. Methods that you were asked about yesterday are discussed here. You were asked questions about this in the examination-in-chief. On page 17, you were asked something about that. It says: "Information on the methods and means for the work of security organs and results obtained by their implication constitute a military secret at the strictly confidential level unless they are classified as state secret. "The officers managing security organs, persons serving in these organs, and other persons who come into contact on whatever basis with information within the competence of security organs are obliged to protect that information according to the regulations in effect on the protection of secrecy. "The obligation to protect information under paragraph 2 of this item continues after the end of service in security organs, or after the end of service in the armed forces." And so on. You were asked many questions yesterday about why a brigade commander did not need to know that one of his soldiers was in communication with someone abroad. You answered that it did not prevent the commander to command such a person like any other soldier. My question is this: In case you informed all commanding officers at all levels, from battalion to the corps, would be -- would there be a greater degree of leakage of information that such measures were applied to a specific soldier than if only one specific officer was informed about that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certain that there would be greater consequence, especially at the lower level than if only the corps commander was informed about this. I said yesterday that I could have informed the brigade commander of the fact that he had a security problem in his unit, that the problem had been noticed, or perhaps a counter-intelligence problem. But until light was shed on this case, and until the character of the activity was fully established, we could not inform the commander of that. Or else, I also mentioned another possibility. If we assessed that he was a sufficiently mature man who realized the nature of security organ's work, then possibly he could have been indirectly told this. Like, for example, Listen comrade, in your unit have you a problem which we are trying to resolve by our methods and means. Once we do resolve it, you will be informed what this is all about. So that was more or less the communication and the mind set that were the basis of such contacts and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber, was any intelligence concealed from a brigade commander if he needed it to command the brigade and the individuals on whom such methods were applied? Did you conceal from him information about the enemy or was it just the methods of your work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It never happened that from a unit commander, at any level whatsoever, from a battalion commander onwards, would not receive information about the enemy, the situation on the front, whatever was of vital importance for the unit. Your Honours, our practice was to receive intelligence from the sector headed by General Tolimir; that is to say, from the Main Staff, and forward them in their original form to the lower levels of command; that is to say, to the brigade commanders and brigade commands, so that they could acquaint themselves in more detail with whatever was happening within and without the corps zone of responsibility. That is to say, this just didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is my question: The brigade commander who was not informed about you applying methods against a soldier who was maintaining communication with a foreign country, was it useful for him to know or not know that you were, for instance, secretly listening to this communication?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit benefitted from this, of course. And how do I mean that? In the sense that you would resolve the security problem. Because if you say that someone was maintaining communication with the enemy side, then, of course, once you eliminated such an individual, the enemy would have one source of information less. And that was reflected in the unit. And personally, as the unit commander, he would have nothing, either positive or negative, from that. Perhaps it would be a negative impact if the activity continued and then a breakthrough of enemy forces may have occurred in one section of the front, for which this individual may have said -- and I'm fast again, I apologise. Where the defence was the weakest and so on. This is the sense in which I mean there could have been a negative impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And were these methods applied precisely to establish whether this individual was doing any harm to the unit and the brigade commander himself?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain something in my answer to this question. The JNA security organs used certain methods in their work. Some of these methods we could apply on a daily basis without any particular approval. These were the methods such as a counter-intelligence assessment, work with an associate, or to try to translate that that meant establishing operative communication and having contacts in MUP. Then also interviews. And we also had other methods of work which violated the privacy and freedom of individuals, such as secret monitoring and recording, secret listening to telephone communications and other communications, secret monitoring of mail, and so on. These were methods for which we needed approval to be able to use them. We needed legal approval, and this was strictly observed. Before the war, such an approval could only be given by an army commander or the federal secretary. During the war, as I said, the commander of the Main Staff and the level of the corps commander could give such an approval. These secret methods were something that we sometimes needed in order to prove or clarify or resolve fully a specific security problem. Essentially such methods exist everywhere. It's no secret that such methods are applied. The biggest secret is who do you apply them to. That is essentially the character of the application of such methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... please wait for the translation to be finished. I would like to get one clarification. You are commenting on the rules of 1984, and you stated at the beginning of your last answer: "The JNA security organs used certain methods in their work ..." You were referring to the JNA. Did these rules for the JNA also apply for the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Yes, these rules were adopted by the Army of Republika Srpska, and they were used in the work of the VRS. This is why in some of my answers I say "the JNA"; whereas, I should actually say "the VRS."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you recall in which way they were adopted for use in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we received a written order concerning this from the Main Staff. It said the rules which had been in force in the former JNA should be applied and have been adopted and are to be applied in the Army of Republika Srpska. At the time, as we were as yet setting up, our structures did not have any specific rules, and considering that the army mainly included officers of the former JNA, then this was a decision that was only logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, now please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Colonel, in the VRS, was the continuity of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia recognised internally and externally through application and abidance by the rules regulations?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It could be an interpretation of the situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could a security organ, at any point apply any methods on his own initiative, including, for instance, the method of opening letters?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was forbidden, and security organs always made sure that checks and controls were applied. We had to abide by the legal framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at Article 50 of the same rules, which can be found on the 14th page of the Serbian and 18th of the English version. Thank you. Article 50 should be on page 31 of the rules. Article 50. Page 20 in the English version. Thank you. Yes, we can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can move the Serbian version to the left so that Article 50 is clearly seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And it is stated there, I'm quoting: "For improper relations in performing duties within their competence and for ... failure to abide by or a violation of the provisions of these rules, officers in security organs are called to account according to the general regulations." My question to you is the following: In such a case, would an officer be brought before either disciplinary organs or criminal or legal organs; in other words, courts?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he would be responsible before them. Not only would such a person be excluded from the activities of the security organs. Persons like that would fall under the measures that are to be applied in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 49, there was quite a lot of mention of the instruction and you said that you would really like to see this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P1112 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Because that is the instructions you were asked about during the interview and also during the direct examination here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: These are instructions on command and control over the security and intelligence organs of the VRS. And we will read just one segment: "Lately, frequent problems, failures, and irregularities have been registered in command and control over the security and intelligence organs at all levels of command in the VRS, diminishing the efficiency of intelligence and counter-intelligence work in the VRS and leading to failures and problems which endanger the security of units and commands. The events observed generally arise from insufficient knowledge about the field of work of these organs and their competencies and authority regarding the VRS by some of the commanders at all levels of command? "With the aim of preventing these and similar problems in control of the security and intelligence organs and creating better conditions for their more effective use, I hereby issue the following instructions ..." And this is my question based off of the text: And let me first ask you whether you remember having received this document at the time it was issued to the units? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what is the difference between instructions, an order, and a directive? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is -- or these are instructions which is something that represents guide-lines; and directive is in -- binding. It's an order. So that's the central difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words this document is neither an order nor a directive. It's just instructions, as you confirmed a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see the following page of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There is eight items in total and once you've had an opportunity to go through them, we'll move to the next page. So you will tell us once you've finished, and then we'll just see the signature as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Next page, please, so that we can see the signature as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I just need you to explain for me again the central difference between an instruction, guide-lines, and directive. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand instructions as a document which provides advice; whereas, directive is an order. I also mentioned a different document, a report or an information, which is a document that presents information. Such an information provides you with a newly obtained information, so I made a distinction between three types of documents. I hope I defined them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, now your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Under item 8, we see a paragraph saying: "Forward these instructions and inform of their contents all commanders of units and institutions, down to battalion level." In other words, this is something which has a purpose of only informing the officers about the rules and regulations for their activities. It is signed by assistant commander which means that the commander wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to ask the e-court to go to the next page. Here we can see item number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "The security and intelligence organs are directly commanded by the commander of the unit or institution of which they form part, but with regard to professional activities they are controlled centrally by the security and intelligence organs of the superior command. This indicates their full independence in the implementation of intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks ..." Is this independence to the effect of command independence in corps and brigades?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. My understanding of the document at the time of the first reading of it, as well as now, refers to independence in security and counter-intelligence activities, because this is where I'm an expert in. I'm not an expert in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If commanders receive a document of this type, is it clear to them that they are not supposed to get involved in the expert line of work of security organs?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the instructions we see before us are a result of some irregularities that had occurred in the period preceding it and had been observed in some units within the process of control and command over the security organs. Namely, some commanders - and I'm speaking of levels above battalion command and battalion commander - there was lack of good understanding of what the activities of security organs should be. There were also some security organs who may have not known or who may have not carried out their duties properly, and this is what I referred to when I said that we were not beyond reach.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The instructions, does that represent expert guide-lines issued to commanders and security organs with a purpose of telling them how to properly apply the rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I understood it. I think we can see it somewhere in the document. The purpose was to remove the irregularities, and with an aim of achieving better co-operation which would benefit the unit and the command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since there was a lot of discussion yesterday about trust or lack of trust during the direct examination, when we look at the document, is this issue what is being discussed in it or is it just about abiding by the law?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of the instructions was that everyone was told to abide by the rules and regulations in their activity and within their competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know from your practice that there were cases where a commander would be against the fact that security organs were informing their professional superiors about problems that can endanger the security of the unit or institution?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going through your documents, documents sent by the Main Staff I mean, not only this set of instructions but other information and reports we received, I received intelligence about some brigade commanders and corps commanders - and I'm talking about that level because they're of main interest here. So I did hear that some commanders would be opening the mail of the security organs, that they would not allow for the codes to be used before they had read the documents, that they would not allow the security organ to use an official vehicle or even a phone. So it was logical, after such events and practice, that the superior institution would issue guide-lines in order to introduce some order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us what would be the reason for brigade commanders to gain insight into reports submitted by security organs in relation to problems within the zone of responsibility of the unit?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding of this is -- well, we have a saying in our language where we say that for some, even war is good. Nobody can say that everyone was clear, and some people even profited from the war. And I believe that the conflicts between people were mainly caused by this trend. Some people were more focussed on their financial gains than on situation on the front. So if a security organ would notice something like that and report about it, then one could -- one would expect a conflict between his superior officer, his commander, and himself, and I believe that that was mainly, almost exclusively, the case. There were units and commanders who were superiors to their relatives, people from the same village, from the same neighbourhood, and maybe some people were treated better than others, and reports were also made about such trends. There were some unit officers who would receive money from people who were not part of the unit. These people would be giving money to commanders so that they don't actually have to be in the unit although the unit would have it on its roster. Security organs would report about that and that was another source of conflict. I don't want to say also that all security organs were people beyond blame, but I believe they were more responsible in their work at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. It is time for a break. Just one last question before that. Were security organs duty-bound to report along their professional lines to their professional organs of their superior command and that they were not doing so because they wanted to work against their own brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, they had to report because that was within their job description. This was not spying on the brigade itself. Such an occurrence would mean that a commander who is suspicious of such activities is completely ignorant of what the work of security organs actually entails. I was trying to explain to the commanders all the time that they were the first element of security in their unit, that it was not us. Anything that goes on in the unit, starting with morale, the situation at the front, people abandoning positions, sabotage. This all goes through them because they were the person number one in good or bad, and we were there to assist them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know we're at the break. I was wondering if we could get an estimate from the Defence as to their remaining time for cross-examination. We have had a witness available to go, and if we're not going to reach him I'd rather not have him sit around for another hour and a half or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was just going to ask Mr. Tolimir as well. Can you give us an estimation about the length of the remainder of your cross-examination? Have you any idea?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I won't need more than 20 minutes, because I had foreseen some time for re-examination. If Mr. Thayer will have no questions, we can immediately continue with the next witness. I can make my questions even shorter, hoping that the witness will provide short answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer, can you indicate how much time you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have two very brief areas, Mr. President. Perhaps five to ten minutes at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it is not very probable that we really can begin with the next witness, perhaps only five to ten minutes. I think this is not appropriate for the witness and for understanding of the whole procedure. In my view, the witness should be released and come back next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn and resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, we looked at the instructions, and we saw they were sent in order to have a better co-ordination between the different organs. We could also see that it came about because there were some reasons to improve the work of security organs, et cetera? Were security organs duty-bound to report only on matters as prescribed by the law and regulations or could they report on just about anything? Perhaps you can tell us, based on your previous work experience with security organs.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, security organs had to work in accordance with the regulations when reporting on only those matters that had to do with the combat readiness of a unit and anything that had to do with the security situation in the unit itself and its area of responsibility. They were not interested in any other information, and they did not report any other information. In any case, I don't see what other matters would be interesting during a war, other than to report on the combat readiness of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday at page 53 of the transcript during examination-in-chief in line 11 you were asked whether you had to report to Tolimir or was it sufficient to report to Salapura, and you said that you reported to the security or intelligence administration and that they in turn most likely informed the commander and that they exchanged information. My question is this: Please tell us clearly, did you have to report directly to me, in addition to reporting to Beara or Salapura, or was it enough to send the report to your superior; and then, that superior, had his obligation, vis-a-vis my position, as per establishment?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I addressed that yesterday, Your Honours. I reported to my first immediate subordinate -- superior. In this case, the security administration, Captain Beara, and the intelligence administration, Colonel Salapura. They, in turn, had their own duties and obligations towards you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you receive some information from your subordinate, from a brigade or corps, do they have to inform you on every single thing they receive from their subordinates or can they decide what things to report to you?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, they did not report on just about everything they received in their battalion reports. They have to make an assessment as to the importance for the security situation of the unit or its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does the same apply at all other levels, such as the level of corps, Main Staff, administrations, and sectors?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was our practice. We used teletype, and, hence, information had to be brief and concise, as well as clear. To achieve that, only the basic elements had to be included. Any detailed reporting could have been done through personal contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If we turn the process around, if we -- there are documents arriving from higher levels, such as the Main Staff and the administrations, does this command principle apply as well, in order to have people informed along professional lines?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's be specific. If I received an instruction, a guide-line, or another document from the -- either security administration or sector that you were the head of, depending on the importance of that information and suggestions, I had to acquaint my subordinate organs with it. That is how such direction was forwarded to lower levels. In such instances, I also suggested to them to convey that information to their subordinate levels, to the level of battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Along both command and professional lines, could superiors ask for the original piece of information used to inform them of events, be it -- whether that information came from the level of battalion, brigade, or any other level?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not clear about the question. What do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's put it this way. If I received a piece of information from Salapura and Beara, after they made their assessment, did I have the right to ask for the original piece of information you had sent to them, in order to have a full insight on how this information was passed on to me?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was also part of the practice we used. If there were any -- if there was anything that was not clear, it needed clarification. If one moves from one level to the next, the information becomes more concise, and if something became clear -- unclear in the process, of course, I could ask for the original piece, to see whether something was omitted when summarising that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the principle of subordination abided by within the command structure and the principle of levels in the professional system when it comes to communication with one's first, second, or third subordinate? Let me put an example. Could I, without your knowledge, address a security organ that is subordinate to you in Kljuc or Petrovac, or did I have to go through you? And the same applies to other levels above yours.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was standard procedure in our army that when a guest arrives, he or she should make it known to the host. In other words, when I went to one of my brigades to see my security organ, I first went to see the brigade commander to let him know that I had come to his unit with a specific intention in mind. And then I would go on working with my subordinate. The same practice was followed by you, and I believe I mentioned that in my earlier testimony in the Beara case. When you came, you first came to the corps command. You made it known to the corps commander. It was only then that I would come to see you or you would come to my office. You also told the commander the reason of you being there. It was only logical when you toured the security organs to have my subordinates briefing you in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday there was some discussion about trust or a lack of trust. You were asked whether some information could be hidden from Tolimir and what the consequences may have been. I'm asking this now: Did Tolimir trust Salapura and Beara enough to believe what they forwarded to him rather than trying to contact -- contact their subordinates? Did he -- did Tolimir accept information he received from them?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was this mutual trust, because they were your closest associates. Subordinates, they were your subordinates who had their own respective security organs. If you hadn't trusted them or if they had falsely informed you, the consequences would have been grave. I would not have an assistant who -- whom I don't trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 62, you discussed the military police battalion, and you said that all reports came to Keserovic who was the chief of MP department in the security administration. My question is this: Did Keserovic have to acquaint Beara, who was his superior professionally, with all of the reports he had received, or could he make a selection of it? Did he have to acquaint his commander with every single piece of information and document he received from the military police?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, he didn't have to forward all the information. He probably made a summary report on the basis of the information he had received from the battalions. He probably made a report which contained -- which contained enough information to paint a picture of what was being done in the various units during that day, such as where the forces were engaged, and so on. It was standard practice that not all reports were forwarded but that a summary report was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier you talked about one organ being removed because of his disagreements with the commander. This is my question: Were there cases when security organs in our services did not inform us about something and concealed something so that the commanders wouldn't be held responsible for that or that some sort of information would not reach somebody else? It could have been for personal fear for themselves. Therefore you may have learned about some things only after the war. Did that happen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the corps' zone of responsibility I did not have such situations because I supported the security organs. At the same time, I had good relations with the brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, D64 is the document that we would now need to see in the e-court. While we are waiting for it to come up on the screen, I have to say that it's a document from the intelligence department of the Drina Corps, and the date is the 19th of July. It is sent to the forward command post --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please slow down with the information because we cannot interpret at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down. The interpreters can't catch everything you are saying if you are so fast. Please continue. And check the date, please. In the list of documents it is said that it is a document from the 12th of July, 1995. Perhaps you misspoke on page 72, line 6.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The document dates from the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And so as not to waste too much time, reconnaissance enabled us to have the information that the Muslims from Srebrenica would decide to carry out a breakthrough. But they wanted to represent this as an attack of the VRS against the demilitarised zone. And when this was learned, there was an order to register all those who surrendered themselves or were taken prisoner or who were leaving the territory but were able bodied. Can we please have a look at the second page now. Thank you. Page 2 says in the second paragraph: "Considering that it is very important to arrest as many members of the shattered Muslim units as possible, or liquidate them if they resist, it is equally important to note down the names of all men fit for military service who are being evacuated from the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. The old BP will brief the MUP organs in their respective zones of responsibility on the information received."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please show the first page in e-court so that the witness could see what I'm asking him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As this was disseminated to all security organs in the Drina Corps, to General Krstic, Colonel General Popovic as the chief, and also the chief of security in the Bratunac Brigade who is the first listed. He said before this Tribunal that he did not receive this document and that he never saw it. Is it possible for a security organ not to receive a document which is sent encoded by telegram? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that something like that is possible. Maybe only if somebody else, the person in charge of encryption, decided not to forward the document, which would be really bad, or if the commander of the unit took the document and didn't give it to the security organ. I did not have such a case in my units, that I did not receive a document that was addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please clarify your question so that we have it clear on the record. You said: "... also the chief of security in the Bratunac Brigade was the first listed." Can you please state the name of this person so that we can have a reference to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Here is the reference: He testified here on the 7th of April 2010, on page 12513, in lines 13 to 14, he said the following: "I cannot say" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please state the name of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about Mr. Nikolic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is all what I wanted -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic said the following: "I cannot say with full certainty, but I think that I did not see this document before." He also said that he was not aware of a report which was sent also on the 12th of July. It was sent on the 9th of June but to Bratunac Brigade, to the commander and others, to take into account about the international law of war on the occasion of taking Srebrenica. And he said on the 12th of April, on one 12620, that is the page: "This order, this document is something I have not seen before." This is an example of how a security organ may sometimes for certain reasons deny that he was informed about something. Did that happen in practice, in the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot talk about the Army of Republika Srpska. I can just say that in my zone of responsibility and the security organs that I controlled, something like that could not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now have a look at what, on the 6th of April, 2011, Mr. Nikolic said for the record. On page 12405 [realtime transcript read in error "12404"], lines 15 to 25, I asked him whether the Muslim men surrendered to you practically on that road, and he answered: "Yes. As we were moving towards Konjevic Polje, at some point after Sandici, Pervani, or I don't know exactly but along that road we caught up with a group of six Muslim men who were walking. We stopped the APC and we got the six Muslims into the APC and then we brought them to Konjevic Polje. We stopped the APC in Konjevic Polje in an area that was in front of the intersection, and I said to Mirko -- or rather, to Mile Petrovic, that the prisoners should be taken to where the others were. "After a while Mile Petrovic returned. I was sitting right there by the intersection. On the left-hand side there is a house when you're coming from Bratunac." On page 12405, in lines 1 to 6, he sayings the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should come to your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it possible for a security organ not to report the superior officer about something for some reason, whether the reason may be fear or something else?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, such reasons should not exist. Perhaps you may not be able to report at a specific moment, because you don't have communications equipment available but it was your duty and you were obliged to report your superiors about what you learned or saw, as soon as you could get hold a piece of communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us see what is in the record. Page 12404, lines 5 to 16, this is what Mr. Nikolic said here before the Tribunal: "I asked him what have you done? And he said there was a yellow co-operative building right there and then there is this small river, and he said that he took these people behind this yellow building and killed them. I didn't go there to see whether he had actually killed them or not. Quite simply, I was sick of everything. I didn't do anything about it. As I've said a countless number of times so far, I didn't do anything about it, and I should have done something about it. I should have reported it Celanovic." It's the lawyer. "I said to Celanovic what happened but I didn't do anything official. I did not take any official measures and I think was supposed to have done so." And my question is this: Because he did not report the incident that he talked about, could anyone who is in professionally or in command terms in charge of this from his brigade or corps, could be deemed responsible and taken to account for this?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say that he did not report, then it's his responsibility. It cannot be the responsibility of his superior in any sense. Because the incident was not known because of the fact that he did not report it. If that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I had this incident in mind because when we talked about trust or lack thereof, there might be a reason not to inform about something for reasons of trust or lack thereof and there may be a reason to conceal something, as it was the case here. Isn't it difficult to take any measures against the perpetrators in such cases if one doesn't even know that a crime has been committed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear to everyone that you cannot do anything if you're not aware that a crime has been committed and if you are not aware of a situation. How can I do something if I don't know that that something did happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know about something that happened in the brigade and if the security and intelligence organ from the brigade failed to inform you about that, can you then take any measures relating to the activity that happened or will the commander hold you responsible for what happened? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I cannot take measures if I don't know that something happened and I have not been informed about that. That means I cannot inform my superior that it happened, because I have no idea it did until someone reports to me about that. Therefore, I cannot be held responsible for something that was not reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Thank you for the answers you gave during the examination. Thank you for everything. I wish you a happy return to your home and family. God bless you. And I hope you may live long and enjoy your old age retirement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has completed its examination and has no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. One correction for the record. On page 76, Mr. Tolimir made a reference to page 12404, in fact it was page 12405 he was reading from. Mr. Thayer, your re-examination please. I hope ten minutes are enough for your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It should be. May we have P01112, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, you were shown this document, these instructions that we saw were issued under General Mladic's name. And if we go to the last page in both versions, I think in your interview and in your Popovic testimony you were able to recognise whose initials or whose signature this was, signing for General Mladic. Do you remember that, and can you tell us who actually signed the -- these instructions on behalf of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Your Honours, it is clearly visible here that the signature is for, there is this word "for" the commander. And below that is General Tolimir's signature. So he signed it in lieu of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And you remember the questions about what the difference is between an instruction and a directive and your answers about that, do you not? That was just a few moments ago, before we broke the last time.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we look -- if we can go back to the first page of this document, we can see that, indeed, it has the heading "Instructions," correct? And when we see, for example, a combat order that will almost certainly say the word "order" or "naredjenje" or -- forgive me for the mispronunciation, but it will say "order," would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you pronounced in properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now if we could go back to the last page in both versions, I want to take you to two paragraphs that General Tolimir did not show you when he used this document with and just give you a chance to look at them a little bit more closely, and I just want to ask you a couple of questions about this. If we look at paragraph 7, let's start with paragraph 7, it says: "Monitoring of the professionalism, legality, and correctness of the work of the security and intelligence organs shall be carried out exclusively by the first superior organs for security and intelligence affairs, except in that part of the their engagement relating to command and staff affairs." And if we look at the next paragraph, it says: "Commanders and other officers at all levels who are in charge of security and intelligence organs must strictly adhere to these instructions." Now, I don't want to focus necessarily on the substance of these two paragraphs. What I want to focus on, for example, in paragraph 7, is where General Mladic uses the word "shall" and in paragraph 8, where, again, General Mladic uses the word "must" when he says that not only security and intelligence officers but commanders must strictly adhere to these instructions. Now, you told us earlier today that - and I quote - this is at page 49, and you were speaking to General Tolimir: "We understood" -- you said: "Perhaps my terminology was a bit rough when I said 'orders,' but this what we understood your documents to be. Anything coming from you or the Main Staff was considered as such." So when General Mladic says, "You shall," and, "You must," did you, as a subordinate officer, feel like you had any choice about the matter?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Your Honours, you are right when you say, "You shall," and, "You must," then it is an order. It is nicely formulated what your obligations are. I mean, your superior formulated it nicely when he says, "You shall," "You must," and he does not say, "I order you" because this is military style or it is more tough. This is nicely formulated. "You shall" or "You must" do that, so it can be translated to mean that it's a sort of order. But as I said, I stand by what I said, that the instruction has the character of advice. It points to a problem and suggests how a problem can be resolved. And this is what items 7 and 8 actually refer to, how to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, though, when we look at, for example, paragraph 8, understanding that what we have here is what has been headed "Instructions," how did you treat, when you look at paragraph 8, this statement that "Commanders and other officers at all levels who are in charge of security and intelligence organs must strictly adhere to these instructions"? Did you have any choice whether or not to strictly adhere to these instructions?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at this paragraph where it is stated that commanders and other officers at all levels who are in charge, this mention of other officers, in my reading, these are the superior officers of the security organ. So the commanders and superior officers of security organs shall strictly abide by the instruction. There is no choice there. You cannot say, No, I will -- No I won't, Yes, I will. You have to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I have just one more quick question, Colonel, and if I may exceed by a couple of minutes, Mr. President. You testified earlier today - this is at page 50 - that: "No assistant at any level, assistant commander, this is what I mean, had authority under any rule, tactical rule, to command forces. Such authority and responsibility lay exclusively with the commander." And for the record that's a proposition that the Prosecution generally agrees with. My question to you, Colonel, is, in your experience, did a commander, whether it be a brigade commander, corps commander, or General Mladic himself, always retain the authority to delegate part of his command authority to someone else?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm, yes. The commander is irreplaceable. That's a fact. The commander could, for instance, when he is absent from the unit for a longer period, when is he away on vacations, when he is ill or wounded, then a written document is drafted specifying who would be in his place throughout that period and what authorities the officer standing in for him will have. In our positive regulation, it was regulated in this way. Also - and I'm now giving examples - when General Milovanovic was standing in for the commander, General Mladic, there was no document where you could find "for" and then Tolimir, as we have here. This type of signature you will find when the commander is absent for a short period, but when he is away for a longer period then it's going to be either "standing in for commander" or "acting commander," let's say Marko Markovic. I don't know whether you see the difference here. When the commander is absent for a longer period, then Marko Markovic is standing in for him and you can see that written. And when he is absent for a short period, then you will see this type of signature "for General Mladic, Tolimir."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think we are all understand the circumstances you are describing, Colonel, but what I want to focus is on a different set of circumstances, not when a commander is taken ill or is outside of his area of responsibility. I'm referring to a situation where a commander may be in a complex situation or a commander can't be in more than one place at a given time. Are you aware of circumstances under which a commander retains his ability to command in his area of responsibility but has multiple tasks that need to be achieved wherein he delegates a portion of his command authority to a designated officer in order to carry out the commander's intentions, with respect to a certain task. Are you familiar with such circumstances, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think there was a little bit of a misunderstanding between you and myself when I was giving the previous answer. Of course, the regulations provided for establishment of forward command posts, of the Main Staff, various corps and so on, along the axis where the commander believed they should be, where the situation is critical. For instance, in the zone of the 2nd Krajina Corps, we had a forward command post of the Main Staff in Drvar, and the top-ranking officer who was there acting on behalf of the commander was General Milovanovic, together with a number of officers from the Main Staff who assisted him in commanding the units of VRS. That was the standard practice, if that's what you were referring to, and such forward command posts would usually be closer to the front lines than the regulations provide for the Main Staff itself. That was a common practice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Colonel Mitrovic, following your testimony, I have a question of a more general nature to put to you. You confirmed that you attended classes on the Geneva Conventions and on the Additional Protocols, you and your colleagues in the security organs. So you are familiar with the laws and customs of war. A while ago, on the transcript, on page 77, line 7 to 9, you said something which struck me. I believe this is extremely important. The security organ could not report on something it knew nothing about. It could not report on crimes it was not informed about. Conversely, crimes it was informed about needed to be reported on. But yesterday on the transcript at page 57, lines 22 to 25, on page 57, lines 22 to 25, you personally regretted the fact that there was no court-martial or war cabinet within the VRS for the period relevant to the indictment. This is an extremely important remark on your part, and I agree with you here. So this is my question of a general nature, Witness. In the event of serious crimes committed by an officer or where a VRS soldier at the time -- or by a VRS soldier at the time, what steps were taken by the security organs and intelligence organs or by any other organ at the level of the corps and at the level of the Main Staff to deal with that kind of situation? Were there any cases of this nature reported? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the measures that were available to security organs in such situations would be, first of all, identifying and finding the perpetrator, then arresting him, and prosecuting him. Or, rather, filing a criminal report to the military prosecutor or military courts. Those were the measures applied in such situations that measures that were approved and measures that could be taken. In my view, that was not very efficient, at least in the segment I'm familiar with, and I mentioned the court-martials from my own perspective, because I believe that their existence would help introduce better discipline in any group or unit. And that was the only reason why I mentioned this. This was what I had in mind when I referred to those courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did such military tribunals exist within the VRS or not?

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to summary court-martials, no, they did not exist. But if you're referring to military court, yes, they existed. They were established, I think, in late 1992, both the military court and the military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You did not tell me whether you had any examples of concrete actions having been reported. In other words, whether crimes were identified and, if so, what had been done about them.

utterances.speaker: MIKAJLO MITROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did mention one such example during the interview with me in 2004. It had to do with murder of prisoners or detainees in the village of Velagici. Investigative organs carried out an on-site investigation, identified the persons, the perpetrators, I think there was 11 or 12 of them, if my memory serves me well. They were arrested, and they were taken to the military court in Banja Luka. I don't know whether this is sufficient by way of example. But that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. That's fine for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you will be pleased that this concludes your examination here in this trial. Thank you very much that you were able to come to The Hague again and to assist us with your knowledge. Now are you free to return home and to your normal activities. Thank you very much again. We have to adjourn, and we will resume tomorrow -- on Monday, quarter past 2.00 in this courtroom, and take the opportunity to thank all the staff who assist us for their patience and for the assistance. Thank you very much. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
